title: The pure in heart (Matthew 5:8)
hook: the pure in heart shall see God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the merciful, and your line was mercy returns. Did you write someone the generous version of their story? Day two hundred thirty-eight, the end of the first week on the mountain.

Count the tabs open on your screen right now. Or in your head. A lot of life happens in split screen: listening to a friend while checking a phone, eating while scrolling, praying while making the grocery list. It's rare to be all in one place. The sixth line of the sermon makes a startling promise: some people will see God. And it says who: not the smartest, not the most religious. The pure in heart.
screen: `COUNT THE OPEN TABS.` → `SPLIT SCREEN.` → `SOME WILL SEE GOD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God." Pure sounds like spotless, never done anything wrong. But the Greek word, katharos, is more like clean, clear, unmixed. Greek writers could use it of clean water, of metal with no alloy, of grain with the chaff winnowed out. And heart, in the Bible, isn't just feelings. It's the center of a person: where you think, choose and want. So a pure heart is an unmixed one. A single heart. Not divided between God and ten other things, not saying one thing and wanting another. The psalm asked long ago: "Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart." In the nineteenth century, the Danish writer Soren Kierkegaard called a book Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. That's close. And the promise: they shall see God. Christians understand that in more than one way. Some look first to a final vision of God, face to face. Others also say the pure in heart start seeing God now: in a face, in bread, in a quiet morning, because they're finally looking in one direction. Look back at this first week on the mountain: Jesus sat down; blessed the empty-handed, the mourners, the meek, the hungry for good, the merciful, and now the single-hearted. Each one is a way of being open.
screen: `KATHAROS: CLEAN, CLEAR, UNMIXED.` · `THE HEART: THE CENTER OF A PERSON.` · `TO WILL ONE THING.` · `SEEING GOD, THEN AND NOW.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL SEE GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing with an undivided heart. For these two minutes, do only one thing: breathe. Nothing else. When your mind opens another tab, and it will, notice it, close it gently, and come back to the breath. You're not failing when you wander. The practice is the coming back. If you pray, you can offer this one undivided moment to God. The bell holds the time.
Katharos, the Greek word for clean, clear, unmixed. A single heart, not split ten ways, and the promise that it shall see God.
Your line: a single heart sees. Today, choose one ordinary thing, a meal, a walk, a conversation, and give it your whole heart, with nothing else open. Day two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray for a clean heart in the words of Psalm 51, and practices like examining the conscience, confession and silent prayer are meant to gather a scattered heart back to one center.

original.note: Greek: the pure, the clean. Matthew 5:8. the singular is katharos.

trapdoor: what you thought: pure in heart means spotless.
what it means: a single, unmixed heart: wanting one thing, and so able to see.
what a scholar hears: katharos is used of unmixed metal and clean water; the verse echoes Psalm 24:4, clean hands and a pure heart.
